flagship_projects.summary: A migration verification tool: proves a migrated PostgreSQL target matches its source by schema, row counts and content fingerprints — built after the shell version it replaced taught me the ways such a tool can quietly lie.
highlights: Rendering settings are pushed in the connection startup packet and read back; the connection is refused if any did not apply, because two servers rendering timestamps differently produce different hashes on identical data.
Rows are sampled by hashing a logical key, never by TABLESAMPLE — physical sampling picks different rows on servers whose page layout differs, even under the same seed.
Runs with row-level security off, so a restricted role makes the server raise rather than silently hide rows and let both sides agree on a wrong answer.
Correctness proven by injecting 18 distinct schema mutations — dropped index, widened column, dropped NOT NULL, redefined view, disabled RLS and more — and requiring every one to be detected.
Ships as a container with Job and CronJob manifests so it can run as a gate inside the cluster it is checking.

case_studies.title: Moving a bank's ledger, and proving it arrived intact
case_studies.hook: 333 GB of regulated payments data moved onto Kubernetes overnight. The move was the easy part. The job was proving, before the country opened for business, that every cent had arrived.
body: A central-bank-regulated payments platform, 333 GB across 17 databases, moving off self-managed PostgreSQL on VMs onto self-managed Kubernetes — a three-node synchronous cluster with a second datacenter for disaster recovery. The migration was physical, a base backup plus streaming replication, so the new cluster ran as a live replica of production for days beforehand. That is what keeps the outage short: cutover is the promotion of a replica that is already caught up, not a restore of 333 GB.

Before any data could move, the platform had to exist — and neither site did yet. Each was built from bare cloud VMs on Huawei Cloud: VPC and subnets, security groups, and VPN access for the engineering team, once for the primary datacenter and again for DR. Five VMs were provisioned per site; four formed a self-managed k3s cluster — three control-plane nodes carrying embedded etcd, plus a worker — and the fifth was held back for separate use. TopoLVM presented node-local LVM volumes so the database writes to disks physically attached to its own node rather than across a network. Backups to object storage and continuous write-ahead-log shipping for point-in-time recovery went in before the first byte of client data arrived.

The rehearsal came first. A full staging migration, then the content gate across every table — row counts plus an order-independent fingerprint over every column — until 4,003 tables verified identical against the source. Only then was a production date discussed.

Cutover went to plan. Writes were quiesced, the source's write-ahead-log position frozen and confirmed unchanged across two samples two seconds apart, replay confirmed caught up, and the new primary promoted. Both standbys re-attached within seventy seconds, synchronous replication intact. The old VMs stayed running as the rollback path — nothing is decommissioned on the night.

Then the part that decides whether a migration is finished. A database that starts is not a migration that worked; the data has to be shown to be right. The gate ran again against the live platform and the ledger tables came back identical — 22,463,214 rows and 493,889 rows, with monetary sums matching to six decimal places, and wallet balances summing identically on both sides. Not a cent had moved.

The same checks surfaced something the database layer never would have: a second copy of the application's background scheduler, still pointed at the old database through the rollback window. An application-tier detail, invisible to every database-level health check, found because the verification compared content rather than trusting that replication had done its job.
The platform opened on Kubernetes that morning, with the ledger proven and the rollback path still standing behind it.
case_studies.tradeoff: The clean 4,003-table figure is the rehearsal, where the source could be frozen. On the night the same checks ran against a source deliberately kept live for rollback, so they function as a health check rather than a pass/fail gate — forward drift on a running source reads as a difference by design. The claim that holds is the precise one: the ledger was proven identical, and everything else was identified and accounted for. Running the comparison early against a live source is exactly what exposed the second scheduler.
case_studies.evidence: Sanity-gate logs either side of cutover (501/507/504 pass, 12/6/9 fail on the main database; 239/238 pass, 8/9 fail on the core-banking database); ledger comparison captured during the incident
case_studies.infra_confirmed: Confirmed by Saurov 2026-10-08: 5 VMs provisioned per site, 4 in the cluster (3 control-plane with embedded etcd + 1 worker), 5th used for a separate purpose. This matches the audited production.conf. Do NOT write '5-node cluster' or '2 workers' - both are false and the real shape reads as deliberate anyway.

case_studies.title: The gate that signed off 4,003 tables
case_studies.hook: Before a regulated migration can complete, someone has to prove the copy matches the original. Building a check trustworthy enough to carry that signature took two rounds of catching the check itself being wrong.
body: To sign off a database migration you need to prove the copy matches the original. Row counts are not enough — they miss changed values entirely — so the check was a per-table fingerprint: an order-independent sum of a hash over every column of every row, which catches a single altered byte anywhere in the table.

Days before cutover it reported a mismatch on the general ledger: identical row counts, completely different fingerprints. The easy response is to believe the tool and go hunting for corruption. The useful one is to ask whether the tool is right.

It was not. The fingerprint hashed each row's *text rendering*, and how PostgreSQL renders a value depends on session settings. The source ran in one timezone, the containers in UTC. Every timestamp rendered differently, so byte-identical data produced entirely different hashes — reproduced deliberately on two servers differing only in that setting.

The fix pins the rendering settings — timezone, date style, interval style, float digits, byte output, monetary locale — identically on both connections, and reports each server's real settings separately so a mismatch is visible rather than silently absorbed.

The next run surfaced a table with *more* rows on the destination than the source. A replica cannot invent rows, so the source was still being written. That produced the second idea the gate needed: a table whose own fingerprint moves between two samples of the same side is classified as live, not as a mismatch — with a strict mode that turns those into hard failures once writes are quiesced for the real cutover.

Later, rebuilding this as a standalone Go tool, the question came up of whether sampling could make it faster. The research reversed the recommendation: the established tools in this space do not sample at all, and PostgreSQL's own TABLESAMPLE samples physical pages — on two servers with identical contents but different physical layout, the same seed returned different rows. So the tool hashes a logical key instead, and both sides select the same rows reproducibly. It also pushes its session settings in the connection startup packet and reads them back, refusing the connection if any did not apply.
With both corrections in place the gate did its job: 4,003 tables verified identical across the full staging rehearsal, and the same mechanism carried through the production cutover.
case_studies.tradeoff: Content comparison is expensive and there is no way around it: a one percent sample and a full scan touched the same 1,248,588 blocks, because the sampling predicate cannot use an index. The honest conclusion was that being both complete and faster than reading every row is impossible for content — only the key set can be verified at full coverage cheaply, via an index-only scan. The tool was built to be correct first and fast second, and says so.
case_studies.evidence: Shell gate used for the migration (three in-cluster variants); standalone Go rewrite with 18 injected schema mutations all detected, 23/23 subtests passing, verified across a PostgreSQL 14 to 16 pair

case_studies.title: One control plane, 2000+ Postgres clusters
case_studies.hook: A single operator replica reconciling every database in the fleet is a bottleneck with a bad failure mode.
body: Built a consistent-hashing shard manager that distributes owned resources across operator replicas, so reconciliation runs in parallel and the ring rebalances when replicas churn.
Fixed three correctness bugs in the hashing library along the way: a division bug, a panic on a single member, and uneven distribution.
Rolled out to provisioner, ops-manager, recommender and Postgres OpsRequests, with a ShardConfig CRD and support for multiple shard keys.
Backed by a large-scale test suite - 8 scripts, 3,557 lines - that bulk-provisions 50 to 1500+ Postgres clusters, benchmarks time-to-Ready, and fires batch OpsRequests across 6 operation types.

related_writing.title: Webinar: Effortlessly provision KubeDB-managed databases at scale using KubeDB Operator Shard Manager

case_studies.tradeoff: Sharding buys parallelism and costs certainty. When a replica leaves the ring its arc is redistributed, so those clusters get picked up and re-reconciled by a new owner — cheap, but no longer a system where one process has the whole picture. "Which replica owns this cluster?" became a question you have to ask before debugging anything. The three correctness bugs I had to fix in the hashing library are the honest measure of how much complexity this adds.

case_studies.title: Zero data loss across datacenters - proved by destroying the primary
case_studies.hook: The test wasn't a failover drill. We deleted the primary with its PVCs and checked whether the other continent still had every byte.
body: Cross-cluster synchronous replication between two KubeDB Postgres clusters, quorum configured as synchronous_standby_names = FIRST 2 (...) so that with a two-replica primary the sync set is always one local standby plus one cross-cluster standby - regardless of which pod currently holds the primary role.

Verification: destroyed the primary cluster with deletionPolicy: Delete, wiping its PVCs. The DR site's content fingerprint was identical, with no promotion performed - the data was durable at commit time, not recovered afterwards.

Found and documented a bootstrap deadlock: enabling synchronous replication before the DR replica is streaming blocks every commit, including KubeDB's own bootstrap writes, so the database never reaches Ready.
case_studies.evidence: kubedb/docs#1038 (+810 lines), validated live on two clusters before the guide was written

related_writing.title: Automating PostgreSQL Operations In Kubernetes Using KubeDB

case_studies.tradeoff: Synchronous replication across datacenters is not free: with the quorum set to always include a cross-cluster standby, every commit waits on a wide-area round trip. That is the right trade for data that must not be lost and the wrong one for peak write throughput, so this is a tier users choose deliberately, not a default. The bootstrap deadlock was the sharpest edge — turning on synchronous replication before the DR replica is streaming blocks every commit, including the operator's own bootstrap writes, and the cluster never reaches Ready. Documenting that ordering constraint mattered more than the feature.

case_studies.title: The cost of always being ready for peak
case_studies.title_note: Quantifiers removed from the title per Saurov, 2026-08-06; customer figures genericized in the body for the same reason.
case_studies.hook: Their only way to survive a campaign was to pay for campaign capacity every day of the year.
body: An e-commerce customer held a multi-terabyte PostgreSQL dataset. Load was modest most of the time but spiked hard during campaigns, when they needed many more read replicas.
Scaling out at that moment meant re-syncing the whole dataset from the primary, per replica - hours to days - so the only safe option was running every replica full-size, permanently.

The fix was to decouple replica count from replica size: keep the replicas running continuously at minimal CPU and memory, streaming, with pgpool load-balancing reads onto them so the primary is no longer permanently over-provisioned.
When a campaign starts, one PostgresOpsRequest vertically scales the existing replicas. No re-sync, because they were never behind. Hours or days becomes minutes.
case_studies.tradeoff: This moves cost rather than removing it. Replicas held at minimal CPU and memory can fall behind under heavy write load, so the design assumes read traffic tolerates some lag. Scaling is a vertical operation, which means a restart per replica — fine with minutes of warning, not something to start when the campaign is already live. And pgpool becomes one more component to run and tune; the connection-exhaustion escalation we later hit traced back to its default pool size.

work_domains.intro: I build and run PostgreSQL on Kubernetes: the operators that manage it, the replication that keeps it alive across datacenters, and the migrations that get it there from self-managed VMs without losing data.
work_domains.framing_note: Four areas, one hard number each. Deliberately NOT a keyword list - the Toolkit section carries keywords, and a list of twelve technologies reads identical to every other candidate's. Do not expand this into prose about 'performance tuning' and similar.
work_domains.avoid: Never use the word 'DBA' for Saurov. He builds the automation that replaces routine DBA work, which is the stronger and rarer claim; 'DBA' invites comparison with career DBAs on query-plan depth, a comparison that adds nothing.

domains.title: PostgreSQL on Kubernetes
domains.body: Provisioning, configuration tuning, scaling, major-version upgrades, TLS and credential rotation, WAL archiving and point-in-time recovery — the whole lifecycle as declarative API calls instead of runbooks.

domains.title: VM-to-Kubernetes database migration
domains.body: Moving production PostgreSQL off self-managed VMs onto self-managed Kubernetes by physical replication, so cutover is the promotion of an already-streaming replica rather than a restore — and proving afterwards that the data arrived intact.

domains.title: High availability and cross-datacenter DR
domains.body: Raft leader election with write-ahead-log positions propagated over gRPC, synchronous quorum replication spanning two datacenters, and an automated promotion path so a surviving site takes over without waiting for someone to notice.

domains.title: Kubernetes operator engineering
domains.body: Go controllers, custom resources and admission webhooks that teach Kubernetes to run stateful workloads it was never designed for, including a StatefulSet fork that places pods across geo-distributed, multi-cloud clusters.

domains.title: Operating it at scale
domains.body: Consistent-hash sharding so one control plane reconciles the whole fleet in parallel, verified with bulk-provisioning benchmarks and deliberate fault injection rather than assumed to work.

domains.title: Regulated and production-critical platforms
domains.body: Banking and payments workloads where the database configuration has to map to a regulator's security guideline clause by clause, audit trails have to survive scrutiny, and recovery has to be drilled and reported to auditor standard.

practices.title: Review is where standards actually live
practices.body: 542 reviews for 37 different engineers. I read for the failure path first — what happens when this call times out, when the pod is killed mid-write, when the field is nil. Style is a linter's job and I don't spend review cycles on it.
practices.proof: 542 reviews · 37 engineers · peak 94 in one month

practices.title: Context beats onboarding calls
practices.body: New engineers lose weeks to knowledge that only exists in someone's head. I write it down instead: per-repository architecture context files, and a tiered troubleshooting curriculum that walks from events-first triage through timeline correlation to root-cause discipline.

practices.title: I own the release, including the announcement
practices.body: Features, stability, production rollout, and the public post — one person accountable end to end. Writing the announcement myself is the forcing function: if I can't explain what shipped, it wasn't ready to ship.

practices.title: Prove resilience, don't assert it
practices.body: I ran fault injection against our own HA Postgres and published what broke, then reviewed the engineers who repeated it for MySQL, MariaDB and Redis. The point wasn't my experiment; it was making 'break it on purpose' a normal thing for the team to do.
practices.proof: 16+ chaos experiments · seeded a team-wide series

practices.title: On-call is a leadership job, not a rota entry
practices.body: Enterprise escalations across six countries land on me. The first move is always narrowing blast radius and establishing a timeline — a root cause that arrives after the customer has given up is worth very little.

k8s_surface.intro: "Kubernetes" on a CV covers everything from applying a manifest to writing the controllers that make new kinds of workload possible. I work at the second end — I build the controller, and it does the job a person would otherwise do by hand.
k8s_surface.note: Kept deliberately high-level per Saurov, 2026-08-07: no informer/workqueue internals, no OCM or ManifestWork. The point is what the controller DOES, in terms a hiring manager understands, while still naming enough real Kubernetes machinery to be credible.

upstream_defects.intro: Two defects found while running the product against a regulated production workload, fixed upstream rather than worked around locally.

items.title: Command injection in Pgpool user synchronisation
items.body: The operator interpolated a secret's password into a double-quoted shell string, so a password containing shell syntax was truncated — and a crafted one executed. Anyone able to create a Secret with two labels in the namespace got command execution in every Pgpool pod. Fixed by passing credentials as positional arguments.
items.found_how: Started as 'why didn't this one user sync?' — the failing password ended in a dollar sign.
items.ref_note: kubedb/pgpool is a PRIVATE repo - never link PR #148. Describe only.

items.title: Point-in-time restore broken for any tuned database
items.body: The WAL-restore sidekick receives no config mount, so every setting from the config secret silently vanishes during replay and recovery aborts on the standby parameter check. Pods report healthy throughout; the only evidence is in one container's log. Fixed by reading the values from the control file instead.
items.found_how: Hit during a point-in-time recovery drill, where it is guaranteed to trigger on any cluster with raised connection or worker limits.
